newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ORBCOMM aims high for "flying computers".
newsitem.headline: ORBCOMM aims high for "flying computers".

text.p: U.S.-based satellite company ORBCOMM Global LP is aiming for up to three million users for its small low-earth orbit (LEO) satellites within seven years.

"We expect globally by the years 2000-2003, there will be between 1.5 to 3.0 million subscribers on the ORBCOMM system," president and chief executive officer Alan Parker told Reuters in an interview on Monday.

A third of that is likely to come from Asia, he said, with another third from North America. On Monday, ORBCOMM announced that Malaysia's Technology Resources Industries (TRI) had signed a licensing agreement to provide satellite services in Singapore, Malaysia and Brunei from 1998.
ORBCOMM is a partnership between Orbital Sciences Corporation and Teleglobe Inc of Canada TRI has a 30 percent stake in Teleglobe.
"We expect one or two more (licensees) this year and then a series over the first six months of 1997," he said. ORBCOMM receives a third of its licensees' revenues from the use of the satellites.

ORBCOMM was talking to would-be licensees in Asia-Pacific and was planning a "regional alignment" in Europe. "We'll probably announce that very soon -- a regional group of...countries in one licensee," he said.

Parker said most of ORBCOMM's small LEO satellites would be about 775 km (485 miles) above the earth and weigh about 43 kg (90 pounds) each, compared to traditional geogstationary satellites that weigh several tonnes and are 36,000 km (22,500 miles) away.
It was also smaller than big LEO systems like Motorola's Iridium satellite that weighs 15 times more and was more expensive to launch, said Parker.

"These (ORBCOMM's) satellites are non-voice, they don't do video but they do the equivalent of two-way alphanumeric paging -- short message or email every place on earth at affordable cost for equipment and for the service. The satellites are like flying computers," he said.
ORBCOMM currently has two satellites in operation and 34 more are being constructed. It will launch 26 satellites in 1997 and the remaining eight will serve initially as ground spares.
It is targetting industries such as petroleum, shipping, trucking, data collection, environmental applications, and recreational uses by hikers and boaters.

ORBCOMM would also provide a search and rescue capability through a global positioning system (GPS) receiver. An industrial device with GPS capability costs US$995 and one without costs US$795. Smaller personal devices without a full keyboard cost US$200-250 each.
ORBCOMM saw itself as complementary to existing communications services.

"We expect licensees like TRI will enter into agreements with paging companies for hybrid services. So you carry one device that not only has a pager but maybe a cellphone and an ORBCOMM unit. When you are in the city, the existing companies like pager and GSM will get the business, when you're out of the city ORBCOMM comes in," Parker said.

ORBCOMM was not competing with geostationary nor big LEO systems like Iridium either. "They are much more expensive." He estimated the minimum usage charge for ORBCOMM to be US 5-25 cents compared to Iridium's minimum charge of US$3 per minute.
Emergency users would probably pay US$50-100 a year while a personal user would pay about US$25-50 a month.
ORBCOMM currently has few subscribers, but would be able to break even with 350,000 subscribers, said Parker.
